newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Strong dlr seen denting soutern Latam trade.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strong dlr seen denting soutern Latam trade.

text.p: Mexico may be closer to the U.S. Federal Reserve headquarters, but more distant Argentina and Brazil are the ones these days feeling the strong U.S. dollar's heat.

As the dollar extends a two-year rally against the mark and the yen, "Latin competitiveness with the rest of the world suffers, with troubles greatest the further south you go," Chief ABN-AMRO Latin American economist Ian Campbell in Amsterdam said.
Enticed by rising U.S. interest rates and escaping low European and Japanese rates, global yield-seeking liquidity are sloshing into U.S. assets, further firming the strong dollar.
That spells little trouble, analysts say, for northern Latin American countries such as Mexico, which sends 80 percent of its exports to the United States.
But further down south in countries with greater trade diversification, dollar strength is denting export competitiveness -- even if the effects are muted so far.
Argentine exports to Brazil are now six times exports to the United States, with trade outside the Americas growing at a rapid rate.

Yet with the Argentine peso pegged one-to-one to the rising dollar "imports become cheaper, and Argentine exports loose against European and Japanese exports to the world," said Macroeconomica consultants' analyst Juan Carlos Falack.

In Chile, currently enjoying a $1.8 billion trade surplus, dollar strength "hasn't affected us very much so far, because our trade balance is looking good ... but down the road we're going to feel it," Santander economist Valentin Carril said.
"If I'm selling salmon to Japan (Chile's No. 1 export market), my buyers might demand a reduction in the price to compensate for the dollar's rise," he added.
Although analysts say the strong dollar is here to stay at least until the end of the year, they note that it pales in comparison to Latin America's trade opening over the past decade.
"Trade liberalization continues to dominate over any strong- dollar trade effects," said JP Morgan economist David Sckiguichi.

In addition, many Latin currencies, used as exchange rate anchors, are appreciating faster than the dollar. This is useful in the fight against inflation, but also a boost for imports at the expense of local production.
"We're suffering a double whammy," Venezuela's Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Boris Molina said.
"The bolivar is strong against the dollar, and the dollar against the rest of the world. It's good for domestic consumption and the feel-good effect, but punishes non-oil exports."
Brazil, which accounts for over one-third of the continent's economy and exports to the United States less than half what it sells to Europe and Japan, may feel the greatest effects.
Exporters grapple with the local currency, the real, which analysts say is between 10 and 20 percent overvalued.
Further dollar strength will add a few watts to the spotlight on Brazil's burgeoning trade deficit seen at $10 billion by year end, analysts say.

Ratcheting up the pain, manufactures dominate Brazilian trade, which are not priced in dollars in the same way as so many Latin American commodity exports, such as Argentine grains and Venezuelan oil.
Brazil needs to slow imports, either through lower domestic absorption or trade restrictions, which will have a chilling effect on Argentine exports, ABN-AMRO's Campbell said.
"The strong dollar and rising U.S. rates will probably slow Latin American growth to around 3.6 percent this year, rather than four or five, mainly because of its effect on Brazil," he added.

In the debt markets, U.S. interest rates are widely expected to rise another 50 basis points before the end of the year and Latin bond issuers have already scaled back U.S. dollar issuance in favor of yen and European currencies.
That has its upside, analysts said.

"By issuing in marks or yen you can attract German and Japanese high-yield chasers," said New York-based IDEA Gene Freida. "Then you can swap into appreciating dollars and service the debt with that ... so a strengthening dollar does have its beneficial effects."
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
